title: Secreted PCSK9 decreases the number of LDL receptors in hepatocytes and in livers of parabiotic mice
authors: Lagace TA, Curtis DE, Garuti R, McNutt MC, Park SW, Prather HB, et al.
population: HepG2 cells, mouse embryonic fibroblasts, transgenic and parabiotic mice; plasma from 72 human volunteers
funder: Grants from the Perot Family Foundation and the NIH (HL-20948 and HL-38049); T.A. Lagace held a fellowship from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada; D.E. Curtis was supported by the UT Southwestern Physician Scientist Training Program.
authorConflicts: J.D. Horton is a consultant for Alnylam Pharmaceuticals, Aegerion Pharmaceuticals, Metabasis, Merck and Pfizer, and is on the Speakers' Bureau of Merck, Merck/Schering-Plough Pharmaceuticals and Schering-Plough.
result: PCSK9 undergoes autocatalytic cleavage in the ER; the cleaved prodomain stays associated with the catalytic domain and the complex is secreted. PCSK9 was independently identified as an SREBP-regulated gene. Plasma PCSK9 in 72 volunteers ranged from about 50 to about 600 ng/ml. In HepG2 cells, 0.5 micrograms per ml purified PCSK9 for 4 hours reduced cell-surface LDL receptors by about 50%; the gain-of-function mutant D374Y was at least 10-fold more active. Uptake of PCSK9 depended largely on LDL receptors; PCSK9 and the receptor associated directly and colocalised in late endocytic compartments. In parabiosed mice, PCSK9 from transgenic partners reduced hepatic LDL receptors of wild-type mice to nearly undetectable levels.
